# Transforming Data

## Load Libraries

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse) 
library(here)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(janitor)
library(plotly)
```

![](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/logo.png){width="10%"}

## Read in Data

We'll continue with penguins for now! We'll read the data in and clean up the column names in a single code chunk below.

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| label: read data

penguins_data <- read_csv("data/penguins_lter.csv")

penguins_data <- penguins_data %>% 
  clean_names()
```

## Interactive Data Visualization

You got a preview of interactive data visualization in the last file (`week03-penguins-data.qmd`), so let's try another example, again with `plotly`.

We'll start by creating a scatter plot of flipper length by body mass with `color = species` and `shape = island`.

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| label: try plotly
flipmass <- ggplot(data = penguins_data, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species, shape = island)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
  
ggplotly(flipmass)
```

Let's add one more variable: `sex`. Can you think of a way to add another dimension of information in these visuals?

Facets help us split a single plot into multiple panels, based on the values of a selected variable. Each panel shows a different “slice” of the data, making it easier to compare patterns across categories.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#| label: try faceting
ggplot(data = penguins_data, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species, shape = island)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~sex) 
#should only be 2 for penguins - means missing values via mistake, typo, or missing
```

Wait. There appear to be four levels of the variable `sex` here (male, female, ".", and `NA`), when we only expected two.

Confirm that by using the `unique()` function.

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| label: unique values
unique(penguins_data$sex)
#confirms data

```

- If we wanted to know the number of penguins in each category for `sex`, we can use `table()`, however this does not include `NA`

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| label: create a table
table(penguins_data$sex)
#NA is missing because table doesn't include NA

```

- We can use the `sum(is.na())` function to count the number of penguins with `NA` as the `sex`

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| label: count NAs
sum(is.na(penguins_data$sex))

```

Let's filter for observations where `sex` is either male or female and drop observations with `NA` in that column, and save it to a new object.

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| label: filter
biological_sex <- penguins_data |> #creating new data set
  filter(sex %in% c("MALE", "FEMALE")) |> 
  drop_na(sex)

#record removal for dplyr
#"c" is combine
```

- Notice in our environment pane (top right) that our \# of observations went from 344 in the data frame `penguins_data` to 333 observation in `penguins_male_female`

Let's make the same style of faceted scatter plot as above frombut with the new data frame. Can you make it interactive using `plotly`?

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| label: cleaned plot

by_sex <- ggplot(data = biological_sex, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species, shape = island)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~sex) 

ggplotly(by_sex)

#2nd plot with islation of sex by island
by_sex2 <- ggplot(data = biological_sex, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species, shape = island)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  facet_grid(island~sex) #Added complexity

ggplotly(by_sex2)

```

Bonus: Instead of `facet_wrap()`, try using `facet_grid(island ~ sex)`. Now you have a grid layout with `island` on one axis and `sex` on the other.

## Data Manipulation/Transformation

Our first plots did not call for us to manipulate the data at all.

How about if we wanted to make a bar graph of the *average body mass by species*? This is a two step process.

1.  Create a new data frame called `average_mass` that has the average body mass for each penguin species. Use the `group_by()` and `summarise()` functions.

```{r}
#| label: avg mass

average_mass <- biological_sex |> 
  group_by(species) |> 
  summarise(average_mass = mean(body_mass_g))
#Created two columns(av.mass/species) and 3 rows(different species)
#Summarize assignment does not have to match initial assignment, can be different name
#group by selective data for group, follow with mutate, summarize, etc

```

2.  Now, create a bar graph using the *new* data frame you made

```{r}
#| label: bar graph of avg mass

ggplot(data = average_mass, aes(x = species, y = average_mass)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") 
#For geom_bar need to tell what to plot on y-axis

```

## Exercise 1

In the code chunk below, create a new data frame called `average_flipper_length` that has the average flipper length for each species.

Bonus: If you assign this to a new object name, you can then use `view(object_name)` to see your results as a table.

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| label: avg flipper length

average_flipper_length <- biological_sex |> 
  group_by(species) |> 
  summarise(flippy = mean(flipper_length_mm))

view(average_flipper_length)
#function allows panel to open up in new tab
```

In the code chunk below, plot `average_flipper_length` using `ggplot()` and `geom_bar`. Customize the graph with colors, a theme, and labels, etc., as you wish.

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| label: plot avg flipper length

ggplot(data = average_flipper_length, aes(x = species, y = flippy, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  theme_light() + #can also use void
  labs(y = "Average Flipper Length (MM)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 50, hjust = 1))
#theme allowed desciption not to overlap
```

## Exercise 2

Create a boxplot of body mass by species & make the plot interactive

- Hints: `geom_boxplot()`, `ggplotly()`

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#| label: mass by species interactive

library(plotly)

ggplot(data = biological_sex, aes (x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .5) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 50, hjust = 1))

p <- ggplot(data = biological_sex, aes (x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .5) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "plasma")

ggplotly(p)
```

## Exercise 3

How many penguins live on each `island`? This one is a little tricky–think outside the box!

- Hint: There are a few different ways, but you can use `summary()` to start.

```{r, message=FALSE}
#| label: count penguins

?summary
?geom_area
ggplot(data = biological_sex, aes(x = species, y = island)) +
  
summary(biological_sex$island)

```

## Note:

Up until now, we’ve mostly *looked* at the data: visualizing it, exploring it with scatter plots and box plots, etc. But in order to answer more specific questions or clean up the data for analysis, we need to actually *transform* it, like filtering out bad rows, computing group averages, or creating new columns. That's where `dplyr` comes in, and that is what Assignment 3 is about.
